questions.q: What are the two main components of 'setting' in a literary text, and how does 'atmosphere' differ from setting?
questions.a: Setting comprises time (historical period, time of day, season) and place (geographical location, physical environment). Atmosphere is the emotional mood or feeling evoked in the reader through descriptive language — it's the subjective experience created by the setting details. A wrong answer that conflates setting with atmosphere (e.g., "setting is the mood") reveals the student hasn't distinguished objective backdrop from subjective emotional effect.

questions.q: In Phoolchand's first poem, the line "xksoqQy rsft eèkqiqj cl js du vitl ysy" (सखी सखी एकएक चल जा दू विटल यस्य) — explain in your own words how this line establishes both setting and atmosphere simultaneously.
questions.a: The line depicts the sakhi (friend) watching the beloved (priya) walk away into the distance during the rainy season (varsha ritu), establishing spatial setting (separation distance), temporal setting (rainy season journey), and atmosphere of helpless longing (the sakhi can only watch, "du vitl" — from afar). A wrong answer focusing only on "rainy season" misses the emotional atmosphere; one focusing only on "watching him leave" misses the seasonal setting that amplifies the viraha.

questions.q: Given this new couplet in Braj: "बरखा बरसत देखि सखी, विरह बिथा बढ़ी अति जाय / बिजुरी चमके घटा घनघोर, प्रियतम न आवत नाहिं" — identify the setting markers and explain how they construct the atmosphere of viraha.
questions.a: Setting markers: "बरखा बरसत" (rain falling — seasonal/temporal), "घटा घनघोर" (dense clouds — spatial/weather), "बिजुरी चमके" (lightning — temporal moment). These construct atmosphere by: (1) Rain = traditional viraha season (varsha) when separation pain intensifies, (2) Dense clouds = visual metaphor for obscured union, (3) Lightning = fleeting hope that illuminates but doesn't last, (4) "प्रियतम न आवत" = the setting's promise (rain brings lovers together) is ironically unfulfilled. Wrong answer listing only "rain and clouds" without connecting to viraha convention shows mechanical identification without literary understanding.

questions.q: Compare how the first and third poems use 'night' (रात्रि/निशा) differently to construct atmosphere. The first poem has "eèkqiqj" (एकएक — alone/lonely) while the third has "Nu&Nu ruq fNu" (नु नु रुक फनु — onomatopoeic night sounds). What does this shift reveal about the progression of viraha?
questions.a: First poem: "eèkqiqj" (एकएक) — night as solitary isolation, the sakhi watches the beloved depart into loneliness. Atmosphere: static, witnessing separation's beginning. Third poem: "Nu&Nu ruq fNu" — night as alive with sounds (crickets, frogs, rain), each sound amplifies the beloved's absence. Atmosphere: dynamic, sensory assault where every sound becomes a reminder. The shift reveals viraha's progression from acute departure-moment to chronic, immersive suffering where the environment itself becomes hostile. Wrong answer saying "both show night is sad" misses the developmental arc from witnessing to embodying separation.

questions.q: A student claims: "Phoolchand's poems use setting merely as background decoration — the rainy season is just when the story happens." Evaluate this claim using textual evidence from at least two poems.
questions.a: The claim is incorrect. Evidence: (1) Poem 1: "xksoqQy rsft eèkqiqj cl js du vitl ysy" — the rainy season journey (varsha ritu) is the traditional time for lovers' meetings in Indian poetics; the beloved's departure DURING this season violates convention, making setting an active agent of betrayal. (2) Poem 2: "lsgks eèkqj cksy lzoufg lwuy lzqfr iFk ijl u xsy" — the rain clouds (मेघ) are addressed directly as messengers (दूत), personified setting that fails its duty. (3) Poem 3: "tyèkkjk" (वज्राकाक — thunderbolt) — the storm's violence mirrors internal agony. Setting is not background; it's a participating character in the viraha drama. Wrong answer agreeing with the claim reveals inability to see setting as functional in pre-modern Indian poetry where nature mirrors human emotion (रस सिद्धान्त).

questions.q: Write a 4-line Braj-style couplet (in Devanagari or transliteration) that uses a seasonal setting (NOT varsha) to create an atmosphere of viraha. Include at least two sensory images.
questions.a: Example: "शिशिर बयार तन झकोरै, प्रिय बिन काटै न रैन / कुहु कुहु कोकिल बोलत सखी, जियरा लागै न चैन" (Winter wind shakes the body, night doesn't pass without beloved / Cuckoo calls 'kuhu kuhu' friend, heart finds no peace). Good answer: uses non-varsha season (shishir/winter), two sensory images (wind on skin, cuckoo sound), maintains viraha atmosphere. Poor answer: "Winter comes, I am sad, no beloved here" — lacks sensory imagery, Braj flavor, and poetic compression; reveals student treats it as prose statement not poetic construction.
